def: To identify an illness by examining a patient.
ex: The doctor diagnosed her with a mild allergy after running several simple tests.
nat: He was diagnosed with diabetes when he was only twenty.

mis.bad: I was diagnosticated with asthma last year.
mis.good: I was diagnosed with asthma last year.
mis.why: The verb is diagnose; 'diagnosticate' does not exist in English.

def: An illness caused by bacteria or a virus entering the body.
ex: She stayed home for a week because of a serious throat infection.
nat: The nurse cleaned the cut to prevent an infection.

mis.bad: I have an infection in the stomach.
mis.good: I have a stomach infection.
mis.why: English usually puts the body part before infection instead of using 'in the + body part'.

def: Redness, heat and swelling in a part of the body, often caused by injury or infection.
ex: The doctor said the pain in my knee was caused by inflammation.
nat: Ice can help reduce inflammation after a sports injury.

mis.bad: My knee has an inflammation.
mis.good: My knee is inflamed.
mis.why: In English you usually say a body part is inflamed, or you talk about inflammation in general; 'an inflammation' sounds unnatural.

def: Lasting for a very long time or happening again and again.
ex: Many people with chronic back pain find that gentle exercise helps.
nat: He suffers from chronic fatigue and often feels tired all day.

mis.bad: My boss is chronic late to meetings.
mis.good: My boss is chronically late to meetings.
mis.why: Chronic is an adjective; use the adverb chronically to describe a verb or adjective.

def: Very serious or severe, and developing suddenly.
ex: She was taken to hospital with acute pain in her stomach.
nat: There is an acute shortage of nurses in many rural areas.

mis.bad: The pain was acute during three years.
mis.good: The pain was chronic for three years.
mis.why: Acute describes sudden, severe problems; for something lasting a long time, use chronic.

def: A medical operation in which a doctor cuts into the body to repair or remove something.
ex: My grandfather needed surgery on his heart last spring, and he recovered well.
nat: The surgery went well, and she left the hospital two days later.

mis.bad: I will do a surgery next week.
mis.good: I will have surgery next week.
mis.why: Patients 'have' or 'undergo' surgery; doctors 'perform' it. Surgery is also usually uncountable.

def: A doctor who is trained to perform operations.
ex: The surgeon explained all the risks to the family before the long operation began.
nat: Her father is a famous heart surgeon in Chicago.

mis.bad: My brother is a doctor surgeon.
mis.good: My brother is a surgeon.
mis.why: Surgeon already means a type of doctor, so do not add 'doctor'.

def: The amount of a medicine that you take at one time.
ex: Take the recommended dose and never exceed it without asking your doctor.
nat: A single dose of this medicine lasts for about twelve hours.

mis.bad: The doctor told me to take two doses by day.
mis.good: The doctor told me to take two doses a day.
mis.why: Use 'a day', not 'by day', to talk about frequency.

def: Treatment that helps someone recover from an illness or a problem.
ex: After the accident, she started physical therapy to walk again.
nat: He has been in therapy for a year to manage his stress.

mis.bad: I do therapy since March.
mis.good: I have been in therapy since March.
mis.why: Use the present perfect with since, and say 'be in therapy' or 'go to therapy'.

def: A professional who treats physical or mental problems without using surgery.
ex: My therapist taught me simple breathing exercises to calm down.
nat: She works as a speech therapist at a children's hospital.

mis.bad: I have a therapeut who helps me.
mis.good: I have a therapist who helps me.
mis.why: The English word is therapist; 'therapeut' is not used.

def: The process of helping someone return to normal health after an illness or injury.
ex: His rehabilitation after the knee operation took almost six months.
nat: The center offers rehabilitation for people with drug problems.

mis.bad: I did a rehabilitation of my knee.
mis.good: I did rehabilitation for my knee.
mis.why: Rehabilitation is uncountable here, so do not use 'a' with 'of'.

def: A break in a bone.
ex: The X-ray showed a small fracture in his left wrist.
nat: She suffered a fracture while skiing in the mountains.

mis.bad: He fractured the arm in the fall.
mis.good: He fractured his arm in the fall.
mis.why: Use a possessive, not 'the', with parts of the body.

def: To injure a joint by twisting it suddenly.
ex: He sprained his ankle while running down the stairs to catch the bus.
nat: I think I sprained my wrist when I fell off the bike.

mis.bad: I sprained my knee bone yesterday.
mis.good: I sprained my knee yesterday.
mis.why: A sprain affects ligaments, not bones; a broken bone is a fracture.

def: A dark mark on the skin caused by a hit or a fall.
ex: The fall left a large purple bruise on her leg that lasted for weeks.
nat: I have a bruise on my arm, but it doesn't hurt.

mis.bad: I have a purple on my leg.
mis.good: I have a bruise on my leg.
mis.why: The noun for the dark mark on the skin is bruise, not 'purple'.

def: Physical harm to a person's body.
ex: The player missed the final because of a serious knee injury.
nat: Wearing a helmet can prevent a head injury.

mis.bad: I made an injury in my foot.
mis.good: I got an injury in my foot.
mis.why: Use get, suffer or have with injury; we do not 'make' an injury.

def: An injury in which the skin is cut or broken.
ex: The nurse cleaned the wound and covered it with a bandage.
nat: The soldier had a deep wound on his shoulder.

mis.bad: The wound is hurting me since Monday.
mis.good: The wound has been hurting since Monday.
mis.why: Use the present perfect continuous with since.

def: To become healthy again, or to make something healthy again.
ex: It took three weeks for the cut on my finger to heal.
nat: Time heals most wounds, even emotional ones.

mis.bad: The doctor healed me of the flu in two days.
mis.good: The doctor cured my flu in two days.
mis.why: Heal is mostly used for wounds and injuries that get better; cure is for treating an illness.

def: Feeling that everything is moving around you, as if you might fall.
ex: I felt dizzy when I stood up too fast after lying on the sofa.
nat: The heat made him so dizzy that he had to sit down.

mis.bad: I am with dizzy since this morning.
mis.good: I have been dizzy since this morning.
mis.why: Use the verb be or feel with dizzy; do not use 'with' before it.

def: A feeling that you are going to vomit.
ex: The medicine can cause nausea, so take it after eating.
nat: She felt a wave of nausea during the boat trip.

mis.bad: I have nauseas every morning.
mis.good: I have nausea every morning.
mis.why: Nausea is uncountable in English, so it has no plural here.

def: A high body temperature caused by illness.
ex: The child had a high fever and a bad cough.
nat: If your fever doesn't go down, call the doctor.

mis.bad: I am with fever since yesterday.
mis.good: I have had a fever since yesterday.
mis.why: Use have with fever, and the present perfect with since.

def: The sudden noise you make when you push air out of your throat.
ex: I've had a dry cough for almost two weeks now.
nat: Cover your mouth when you cough or sneeze.

mis.bad: I am coughing since three days.
mis.good: I have had a cough for three days.
mis.why: Use the present perfect with for, and the noun cough describes the illness.

def: Protected against a disease because your body can fight it.
ex: After the first infection, most people are immune to the virus for a while.
nat: A healthy diet helps keep your immune system strong.

mis.bad: I am immune of this disease.
mis.good: I am immune to this disease.
mis.why: The correct preposition after immune is 'to'.

def: A medicine that kills bacteria and cures infections.
ex: The doctor prescribed an antibiotic for my ear infection and told me to rest.
nat: Antibiotics do not work against viruses such as the common cold.

mis.bad: I took a antibiotic for ten days.
mis.good: I took an antibiotic for ten days.
mis.why: Use 'an' before a vowel sound, and note that antibiotic starts with the vowel sound /æ/.

def: A medicine that reduces or removes pain.
ex: I took a painkiller and went to bed early because my head hurt so much.
nat: The dentist gave me painkillers to take after the operation.

mis.bad: I took an anti-pain for my headache.
mis.good: I took a painkiller for my headache.
mis.why: The common English word is painkiller, not 'anti-pain'.

def: A strip of cloth used to cover and protect an injury.
ex: The nurse wrapped a clean bandage around his injured hand.
nat: Keep the bandage dry and change it every day.

mis.bad: She put a bandage in the cut.
mis.good: She put a bandage on the cut.
mis.why: Use 'on' for something placed on the skin.

def: A fatty substance in the blood that can cause heart problems when levels are too high.
ex: My doctor told me to eat less fried food to lower my cholesterol.
nat: High cholesterol can increase the risk of heart disease.

mis.bad: My cholesterol are high.
mis.good: My cholesterol is high.
mis.why: Cholesterol is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

def: A condition in which a person is extremely overweight in a way that harms health.
ex: Childhood obesity has become a serious problem in many countries.
nat: Doctors link obesity with a higher risk of diabetes.

mis.bad: Obesity are growing in my country.
mis.good: Obesity is growing in my country.
mis.why: Obesity is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb.

def: A disease in which the body cannot control the level of sugar in the blood.
ex: My uncle has diabetes, so he checks his blood sugar every morning.
nat: Regular exercise can lower the risk of type two diabetes.

mis.bad: Diabetes are common in my family.
mis.good: Diabetes is common in my family.
mis.why: Diabetes ends in -s but is a singular, uncountable noun.

def: A vehicle that takes sick or injured people to the hospital.
ex: Someone called an ambulance as soon as the accident happened.
nat: The ambulance arrived within five minutes.

mis.bad: Call to the ambulance, please!
mis.good: Call an ambulance, please!
mis.why: The verb call takes the object directly, without 'to', when you summon someone.

def: A sudden serious situation that needs immediate action.
ex: In an emergency, dial the number on the card next to the phone.
nat: The hospital's emergency room was full on Friday night.

mis.bad: It is an emergence, call the doctor!
mis.good: It is an emergency, call the doctor!
mis.why: Emergence means 'coming out'; the word for a crisis is emergency.

def: A routine medical examination to check that you are healthy.
ex: I have a medical checkup every year, just to be safe.
nat: The dentist said everything looked fine at my last checkup.

mis.bad: I made a check-up of my health yesterday.
mis.good: I had a checkup yesterday.
mis.why: We 'have' or 'get' a checkup; we do not 'make' one of our health.

def: Medical care given to a patient for an illness or injury.
ex: The treatment lasted six months, but she made a full recovery.
nat: He is receiving treatment for a heart problem.

mis.bad: I am in treatment of a cold.
mis.good: I am getting treatment for a cold.
mis.why: Use treatment for an illness, not 'of'.

def: The process of getting better after an illness or a difficult period.
ex: His recovery after the operation was faster than the doctors expected.
nat: We wish you a quick recovery and hope to see you soon.

mis.bad: I wish you a fast recuperation.
mis.good: I wish you a quick recovery.
mis.why: 'Recuperation' is rare in English; recovery is the natural word, usually with quick or full.

def: The physical or mental strength that lets you keep doing something for a long time.
ex: Marathon runners need great stamina to finish the race without stopping to rest.
nat: I don't have the stamina to work twelve hours a day.

mis.bad: I don't have the resistance to run for an hour.
mis.good: I don't have the stamina to run for an hour.
mis.why: For lasting physical energy use stamina or endurance, not 'resistance'.

def: Having lost too much water from the body.
ex: The hikers were dehydrated after walking all day in the sun.
nat: Drink more water, because you look slightly dehydrated.

mis.bad: I am desidrated after the run.
mis.good: I am dehydrated after the run.
mis.why: The English word is dehydrated, spelled with a 'y'.

def: A substance that plants or animals need to live and grow.
ex: Fresh vegetables are full of important nutrients that help your body stay strong and healthy.
nat: The soil lacks nutrients, so the plants grow slowly.

mis.bad: This food has many nutrients substances.
mis.good: This food is rich in nutrients.
mis.why: Nutrient already means a substance, so do not add 'substances'.

def: A unit that measures the energy in food.
ex: One small chocolate bar has about two hundred calories, which is quite a lot.
nat: If you want to lose weight, you should count calories.

mis.bad: This cake has much calories.
mis.good: This cake has a lot of calories.
mis.why: Calories is countable, so use many or a lot of, not much.

def: A substance in food such as meat, eggs and beans that helps the body grow.
ex: Eggs, beans and fish are all good sources of protein for a healthy diet.
nat: Athletes often eat extra protein after training.

mis.bad: Eggs are a good source of proteine.
mis.good: Eggs are a good source of protein.
mis.why: The English spelling is protein, with no final -e.

def: The chemical processes in the body that change food into energy.
ex: Some people have a fast metabolism and can eat a lot without gaining weight.
nat: Exercise can speed up your metabolism.

mis.bad: My metabolic is very slow.
mis.good: My metabolism is very slow.
mis.why: Metabolic is an adjective; the noun is metabolism.

def: The way you hold your body when you sit or stand.
ex: Sitting at a desk all day can ruin your posture.
nat: Good posture helps prevent back pain.

mis.bad: I need to correct my position when I sit.
mis.good: I need to correct my posture when I sit.
mis.why: For the way you hold your body, use posture, not 'position'.

def: The ability to continue doing something difficult for a long time.
ex: Long-distance swimming requires great endurance, patience and months of regular training in the pool.
nat: Cycling every day will improve your endurance.

mis.bad: He has a big resistance in the race.
mis.good: He has great endurance in the race.
mis.why: For long physical effort use endurance; 'resistance' means opposing something.

def: Spending a lot of time sitting down and not being physically active.
ex: A sedentary lifestyle can lead to serious health problems later in life.
nat: Office workers often have sedentary jobs.

mis.bad: I have a sedentarian life.
mis.good: I have a sedentary life.
mis.why: The adjective is sedentary; 'sedentarian' is not used.

def: The state of being healthy, comfortable and happy.
ex: Regular sleep is essential for your physical and mental wellbeing.
nat: The company cares about the wellbeing of its employees.

mis.bad: I want to promote my well-being state.
mis.good: I want to promote my wellbeing.
mis.why: Wellbeing already means a state; do not add 'state'.

def: A return of an illness after a period of improvement.
ex: He had a relapse and had to go back to the hospital.
nat: The doctor warned her that a relapse was possible.

mis.bad: I had a recaid last week.
mis.good: I had a relapse last week.
mis.why: The English noun for recaída is relapse.

def: Able to be passed from one person to another by touch or close contact.
ex: The flu is highly contagious, so please stay at home.
nat: Her laugh was so contagious that everyone started laughing.

mis.bad: The cold is contagiosa.
mis.good: The cold is contagious.
mis.why: English adjectives do not change for gender, so contagious has one form.

def: Practices such as washing that keep you clean and healthy.
ex: Good hand hygiene can stop the spread of many diseases.
nat: Restaurants must follow strict rules on food hygiene.

mis.bad: I follow the hygienic of my body.
mis.good: I follow good personal hygiene.
mis.why: Hygiene is the noun; hygienic is an adjective.

def: A period of isolation to stop a disease from spreading.
ex: Travelers had to stay in quarantine for ten days after arriving in the country.
nat: Several students are in quarantine after the outbreak.

mis.bad: I stayed in quarentena for two weeks.
mis.good: I stayed in quarantine for two weeks.
mis.why: The English spelling is quarantine, with an 'a' in the second syllable.

def: A sudden widespread outbreak of a disease in a community.
ex: The city launched a campaign to stop the flu epidemic.
nat: Experts fear an epidemic of obesity in the next decade.

mis.bad: There is an epidemy in the region.
mis.good: There is an epidemic in the region.
mis.why: The noun is epidemic; 'epidemy' is not used.

def: A disease that spreads across many countries at the same time.
ex: The pandemic changed the way many companies think about remote work.
nat: Scientists are studying how the pandemic started.

mis.bad: In the pandemia, I worked from home.
mis.good: During the pandemic, I worked from home.
mis.why: Say pandemic in English, and use 'during' for the period of time.

def: An idea that is suggested as an explanation and that must be tested.
ex: The scientists tested their hypothesis with a series of careful experiments.
nat: Her hypothesis was that plants grow faster with more light.

mis.bad: We have two hypothesis to test.
mis.good: We have two hypotheses to test.
mis.why: The plural of hypothesis is hypotheses, with a change in the ending.

def: A scientific test done to learn something or to prove an idea.
ex: In class, we did an experiment to see how salt affects ice.
nat: The experiment failed, but we learned something important.

mis.bad: We made an experiment in the lab.
mis.good: We did an experiment in the lab.
mis.why: The usual verbs with experiment are do, carry out or conduct, not 'make'.

def: A room or building with equipment for scientific work.
ex: The new vaccine was developed in a university laboratory over several difficult years.
nat: She spends most of her day working in the laboratory.

mis.bad: I work in a laboratorium.
mis.good: I work in a laboratory.
mis.why: The English word is laboratory, often shortened to lab.

def: An idea or set of ideas that explains something.
ex: Einstein's theory of relativity changed the way we understand space and time.
nat: In theory, the plan should work, but we need to test it.

mis.bad: I read a very interesting theorie about the origin of the universe.
mis.good: I read a very interesting theory about the origin of the universe.
mis.why: The English spelling is theory, ending in -y; the plural is theories.

def: A person who studies a subject carefully to discover new facts.
ex: The researchers published their results in a well-known science magazine.
nat: She works as a researcher at the national space agency.

mis.bad: The researchers says that the results are clear.
mis.good: The researchers say that the results are clear.
mis.why: A plural subject like researchers needs the plural verb form 'say'.

def: The smallest unit of a substance, made of two or more atoms.
ex: A water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
nat: Scientists can now see individual molecules with powerful microscopes.

mis.bad: A molecule of water have three atoms.
mis.good: A molecule of water has three atoms.
mis.why: The subject molecule is singular, so use 'has'.

def: The smallest part of a chemical element.
ex: An atom is so small that you cannot see it with the naked eye.
nat: Everything around us is made of atoms.

mis.bad: The atoms is very small.
mis.good: Atoms are very small.
mis.why: The plural noun atoms takes the plural verb are.

def: The force that pulls objects toward the earth.
ex: Without gravity, we would all float away from the ground and into space.
nat: The moon has less gravity than the Earth.

mis.bad: The gravity of Moon is weaker.
mis.good: The gravity of the Moon is weaker.
mis.why: Names like the Moon, the Earth and the Sun usually take 'the'.

def: A substance that is made by or used in chemistry.
ex: Some cleaning products contain dangerous chemicals, so you should always read the labels carefully.
nat: The factory was fined for releasing toxic chemicals into the river.

mis.bad: I am allergic to chemic products.
mis.good: I am allergic to chemical products.
mis.why: The word is chemical; 'chemic' does not exist.

def: What happens when substances combine, or how someone responds to something.
ex: My first reaction to the news was surprise, and then I felt very happy.
nat: Mixing these two liquids causes a strong chemical reaction.

mis.bad: I had a reaction of the medicine.
mis.good: I had a reaction to the medicine.
mis.why: Reaction is followed by 'to', not 'of'.

def: The slow change of living things over many generations.
ex: Darwin's work explained the evolution of species over millions of years.
nat: The evolution of mobile phones has been amazing.

mis.bad: I study the Evolution of animals in the school.
mis.good: I study the evolution of animals at school.
mis.why: Evolution is not capitalized in the middle of a sentence.

def: The remains of an ancient plant or animal that have turned into rock.
ex: Scientists found a fossil of a giant bird in the desert.
nat: Fossils help us understand life on Earth millions of years ago.

mis.bad: I saw a fossile in the museum.
mis.good: I saw a fossil in the museum.
mis.why: The English spelling is fossil, with no final -e.

def: A living thing, especially a very small one.
ex: Bacteria are tiny organisms that can live almost anywhere on Earth, even in boiling water.
nat: This organism lives in the deep ocean.

mis.bad: The organisms live in water since millions of years.
mis.good: The organisms have lived in water for millions of years.
mis.why: Use the present perfect with for and a period of time.

def: Very small living things that can cause disease or be useful.
ex: Some bacteria are harmful, but others help us digest food.
nat: Heat kills most bacteria in food.

mis.bad: A bacteria can cause an infection.
mis.good: A bacterium can cause an infection.
mis.why: Bacteria is the plural; the singular is bacterium.

def: A tiny living thing that causes diseases and spreads from one person to another.
ex: The virus spread quickly through the small town, and the schools had to close.
nat: Washing your hands can protect you from the virus.

mis.bad: I have caught a virus of the flu.
mis.good: I have caught the flu virus.
mis.why: Say flu virus, putting the noun flu before virus.

def: A part of a cell that controls a physical characteristic passed from parents to children.
ex: Scientists found a gene that makes some people more likely to get this disease.
nat: She has inherited the gene for red hair from her grandmother.

mis.bad: I have the gens of my father.
mis.good: I have my father's genes.
mis.why: The English word is gene, and its plural is genes.

def: A tool shaped like a tube that makes distant objects look closer.
ex: He looked at the moon through his new telescope and could see the craters clearly.
nat: The space telescope sent back amazing pictures of distant galaxies.

mis.bad: I saw the stars with a telescopy.
mis.good: I saw the stars with a telescope.
mis.why: The noun is telescope; 'telescopy' is a rare technical word.

def: A very large group of stars and planets.
ex: Our solar system is part of a galaxy called the Milky Way.
nat: Astronomers have discovered thousands of new galaxies this year.

mis.bad: The galaxy are very far from us.
mis.good: The galaxies are very far from us.
mis.why: The singular galaxy needs 'is'; with are you must use the plural galaxies.

def: To move around a larger object such as a planet or the sun.
ex: The Earth orbits the sun once every year, which is why we have seasons.
nat: The space station orbits our planet every ninety minutes.

mis.bad: The Earth orbits around of the sun.
mis.good: The Earth orbits the sun.
mis.why: Orbit takes a direct object, and 'around of' is not correct English.

def: A large round object in space that moves around a star.
ex: Mars is often called the red planet because of its color.
nat: We must protect our planet for future generations.

mis.bad: Mars is a planet more small than the Earth.
mis.good: Mars is a smaller planet than the Earth.
mis.why: Short adjectives take -er, and the comparative adjective goes before the noun.

def: A piece of equipment that makes very small things look bigger.
ex: Under the microscope, the cells looked like tiny green dots.
nat: The students used a microscope to look at a drop of water.

mis.bad: I looked at it on the microscope.
mis.good: I looked at it under the microscope.
mis.why: We look at things 'under' a microscope, not 'on' it.

def: To watch something carefully in order to learn about it.
ex: The scientists observed the animals for six months before writing their report.
nat: Children often learn by observing adults.

mis.bad: He observed me that the door was open.
mis.good: He pointed out to me that the door was open.
mis.why: Observe means watch or notice; it does not take a person as an indirect object like 'tell'.

def: To find a number or an amount by using mathematics.
ex: Can you calculate how much we will spend on the trip?
nat: The program can calculate your taxes in a few seconds.

mis.bad: I calculated wrong the bill.
mis.good: I calculated the bill wrong.
mis.why: The object of the verb comes right after it, before an adverb like wrong.

def: To examine something carefully in order to understand it.
ex: The team analyzed the data before they made a final decision.
nat: We need to analyze why sales fell last month.

mis.bad: We need to analyse about the problem.
mis.good: We need to analyze the problem.
mis.why: Analyze is transitive, so do not use 'about' after it.

def: A factor that can change in an experiment or a calculation.
ex: In the experiment, temperature was the only variable that we changed.
nat: There are too many variables to predict the result.

mis.bad: The weather is one variable that we cannot control it.
mis.good: The weather is one variable that we cannot control.
mis.why: Do not repeat the object with 'it' inside the relative clause.

def: A small amount of something used to test or show what the whole is like.
ex: The nurse took a blood sample to check for infections.
nat: A larger sample would give us more reliable results.

mis.bad: The nurse took a sample of my blood sample.
mis.good: The nurse took a sample of my blood.
mis.why: Do not repeat sample; say a blood sample or a sample of blood.

def: Correct and without mistakes.
ex: The weather forecast was accurate, so we took our umbrellas.
nat: Please make sure that the numbers in the report are accurate.

mis.bad: The clock is accurated.
mis.good: The clock is accurate.
mis.why: Accurate is already an adjective; it has no -ed form.

def: Exact and clear in every detail.
ex: The instructions were so precise that anyone could follow them.
nat: Can you be more precise about the time of the meeting?

mis.bad: I need a precise of the time.
mis.good: I need the precise time.
mis.why: Precise is an adjective, so use it before a noun, not as a noun.

def: A new thing that someone has made for the first time.
ex: The invention of the printing press changed the world and made books much cheaper.
nat: The telephone was one of the greatest inventions of the nineteenth century.
col: necessity is the mother of invention

mis.bad: The inventation of the wheel changed human history.
mis.good: The invention of the wheel changed human history.
mis.why: The noun is invention; there is no word 'inventation'.

def: To create something that did not exist before.
ex: Who invented the first telephone, and how did people react to it at the time?
nat: He invented a simple tool to open bottles.

mis.bad: He discovered the telephone in 1876.
mis.good: He invented the telephone in 1876.
mis.why: You invent something new, but you discover something that already existed.

def: To find the size, amount or degree of something.
ex: We measured the room carefully before buying the new sofa for the living room.
nat: This tool measures the temperature of the air.

mis.bad: I measure 1.80 meters of height.
mis.good: I am 1.80 meters tall.
mis.why: To give a person's height, use be + tall; measure is not used like this.

def: To change from a liquid into a gas.
ex: The water slowly evaporated from the pan in the sun.
nat: Leave the plate in the sun and the water will evaporate.

mis.bad: The water evaporated for the air.
mis.good: The water evaporated into the air.
mis.why: The right preposition after evaporate is 'into'.

def: A gas in the air that people and animals need to breathe.
ex: Plants produce oxygen during the day, and we need it to breathe and stay alive.
nat: Climbers carry extra oxygen when they climb very high mountains.

mis.bad: The oxigen is necessary for life.
mis.good: Oxygen is necessary for life.
mis.why: The spelling is oxygen, with a 'y', and no article is needed in this general statement.

def: Energy sent out in the form of waves or small particles.
ex: The doctor explained that X-rays use a very small amount of radiation.
nat: Sunscreen protects your skin from harmful radiation.

mis.bad: I was exposed to the radiations.
mis.good: I was exposed to radiation.
mis.why: In this meaning radiation is uncountable and has no plural.

def: A mathematical statement that two things are equal.
ex: She solved the equation in less than a minute, and the whole class was impressed.
nat: Money is only one part of the equation when you choose a job.

mis.bad: I didn't understand the equacion.
mis.good: I didn't understand the equation.
mis.why: The English word ends in -tion, not -cion.

def: A set of letters or numbers that shows a rule in mathematics or science.
ex: The chemical formula for water is H2O, and every student learns it at school.
nat: There is no simple formula for success.

mis.bad: The formula of the water is H2O.
mis.good: The formula for water is H2O.
mis.why: Use 'formula for' with a substance, and no article before water in general.

def: A person who studies science and does scientific research.
ex: The scientist explained her discovery in simple language so that everyone could understand it.
nat: My cousin wants to become a scientist when she grows up.

mis.bad: My sister is scientific and works in a lab.
mis.good: My sister is a scientist and works in a lab.
mis.why: Scientific is an adjective; the person is a scientist.

def: An object that attracts iron and some other metals.
ex: The child picked up the nails with a small magnet.
nat: Cities with good jobs act as a magnet for young people.

mis.bad: I put an iman on the fridge.
mis.good: I put a magnet on the fridge.
mis.why: The English word is magnet, not 'iman'.

def: A talk given to a group of students or an audience about a subject.
ex: The professor gave an interesting lecture about modern architecture, and many students took notes.
nat: I missed the lecture because my bus was late.

mis.bad: I assisted the lecture yesterday.
mis.good: I attended the lecture yesterday.
mis.why: 'Assist' means to help; to be present at an event, use attend.

def: A teacher at a university or college.
ex: Our lecturer gave us extra time to finish the project.
nat: She is a lecturer in economics at a large university.

mis.bad: My lecturer of history is very strict.
mis.good: My history lecturer is very strict.
mis.why: Put the subject before the noun: history lecturer, not 'lecturer of history'.

def: A small class where students discuss a subject with a teacher.
ex: We had a seminar on climate change at the end of the semester.
nat: The company organizes a seminar on safety every year.

mis.bad: I presented a seminary at the university.
mis.good: I presented a seminar at the university.
mis.why: A seminary is a school for training priests; the word for a class is seminar.

def: One of two periods into which a school or university year is divided.
ex: I will study abroad during the next semester, so I am saving some money.
nat: He failed two classes in his first semester.

mis.bad: I will graduate in the second semester of the next year.
mis.good: I will graduate in the second semester of next year.
mis.why: Do not use 'the' before 'next year'.

def: To finish your studies at a school or university and receive a degree.
ex: She graduated from the university with a degree in biology.
nat: He will graduate next year and start looking for a job.

mis.bad: I graduated in the University of Texas.
mis.good: I graduated from the University of Texas.
mis.why: The preposition after graduate is 'from', not 'in'.

def: An official paper that shows you have finished a course of study.
ex: He proudly showed his diploma to his parents on the day of the ceremony.
nat: You need a high school diploma to apply for this job.

mis.bad: I have a diploma of engineer.
mis.good: I have a diploma in engineering.
mis.why: Use 'diploma in' + the subject, not 'of' + a person.

def: A long piece of writing on a subject, done for a university degree.
ex: She spent a year writing her dissertation on renewable energy.
nat: He has to hand in his dissertation by the end of May.

mis.bad: I presented my dissertation with the committee.
mis.good: I presented my dissertation to the committee.
mis.why: You present something to a person or group, not 'with' them.

def: A long piece of research written for a university degree, or the main idea of an argument.
ex: His thesis argues that cities should invest more in public transport.
nat: She is writing a thesis about animal behavior.

mis.bad: The thesis of my sister is about birds.
mis.good: My sister's thesis is about birds.
mis.why: With people, English prefers the possessive form: my sister's thesis.

def: Copying someone else's work and saying that it is your own.
ex: The student failed the whole course because of plagiarism in her final essay.
nat: Universities use software to detect plagiarism in essays.

mis.bad: He was accused of plagiarize.
mis.good: He was accused of plagiarism.
mis.why: After the preposition 'of', use the noun plagiarism, not the verb.

def: A list of the subjects that will be studied in a course.
ex: The syllabus includes ten books and three written exams, so we have a lot of work.
nat: Please read the syllabus before the first class.

mis.bad: The syllabus of the exam was very long.
mis.good: The syllabus for the course was very long.
mis.why: A syllabus belongs to a course, not to an exam.

def: A teacher who gives extra lessons to one student or a small group.
ex: I hired a tutor to help me prepare for the math exam.
nat: My tutor explained the problem in a much simpler way.

mis.bad: I need a particular teacher for English.
mis.good: I need a private tutor for English.
mis.why: 'Particular' does not mean private; say private tutor or private teacher.

def: The ability to read and write.
ex: The government started a program to improve literacy in rural areas.
nat: Digital literacy is now an important skill for most jobs.

mis.bad: The literacy is low in my city.
mis.good: Literacy is low in my city.
mis.why: Use no article before general uncountable nouns like literacy.

def: A mark that shows how well a student has done.
ex: I got a very good grade on my history test, and my parents were proud.
nat: Her grades improved a lot after she started studying every day.

mis.bad: I took a good note in the exam.
mis.good: I got a good grade on the exam.
mis.why: In English, school marks are called grades; 'note' is a false friend of 'nota'.

def: A short piece of writing on a particular subject.
ex: We have to write a five-hundred-word essay about the environment by next Friday.
nat: The teacher said my essay was clear and well organized.

mis.bad: I did a redaction for my English class.
mis.good: I wrote an essay for my English class.
mis.why: 'Redaction' means editing; a school writing task is an essay.

def: A formal test of what you have learned.
ex: The final exam covers everything we studied this year, so I need to start revising.
nat: I stayed up all night studying for my chemistry exam.

mis.bad: I did an exam yesterday and I passed.
mis.good: I took an exam yesterday and I passed.
mis.why: We take or sit an exam; 'make' or 'do' an exam sounds like you wrote it.

def: To study again what you have already learned before an exam.
ex: She revised all her notes before the exam and felt much more confident afterwards.
nat: I need to revise the whole chapter tonight.

mis.bad: I need to revise for the test the whole day.
mis.good: I need to revise for the test all day.
mis.why: Use 'all day', not 'the whole day', after a time expression of that type.

def: To learn something so well that you can remember it exactly.
ex: I memorized twenty new words before the test, but I forgot half of them later.
nat: Actors have to memorize a lot of lines.

mis.bad: I memorized by heart the poem.
mis.good: I memorized the poem.
mis.why: Memorize already means learn by heart, so 'by heart' is redundant.

def: The ability to understand something.
ex: The test has a reading comprehension section with five short texts.
nat: His comprehension of the topic was excellent.

mis.bad: I have a good understanding of reading.
mis.good: I have good reading comprehension.
mis.why: Reading comprehension is the usual phrase for the skill of understanding a text.

def: All the words that a person knows or uses in a language.
ex: Reading every day is a great way to expand your vocabulary.
nat: My vocabulary in Spanish is still very limited.

mis.bad: I need to learn more vocabularies.
mis.good: I need to learn more vocabulary.
mis.why: Vocabulary is uncountable in this sense, so it has no plural.

def: The ability to speak or write a language easily and well.
ex: Daily practice will help you reach fluency in English faster than you expect.
nat: Her fluency in three languages impressed the interviewers.

mis.bad: I have fluence in English.
mis.good: I have fluency in English.
mis.why: The correct spelling is fluency, ending in -cy.

def: To judge the quality, amount or value of something.
ex: Teachers assess students through tests, class projects and oral presentations throughout the school year.
nat: We need to assess the risks before we start the project.

mis.bad: The teacher assessed me to sit down.
mis.good: The teacher told me to sit down.
mis.why: Assess means to judge or evaluate; it cannot be followed by an infinitive like 'tell'.

def: A judgment about the quality or value of something.
ex: The final assessment includes a written test and an oral presentation.
nat: The company made an honest assessment of its financial situation.

mis.bad: I fear the assessments of the school.
mis.good: I am nervous about the school assessments.
mis.why: Be nervous about something; this is more natural than 'fear' here.

def: The fact of being present at a place or an event.
ex: Attendance at the lectures is not compulsory, but most students go to every one.
nat: Our teacher checks attendance at the start of every class.

mis.bad: My attendance in the course is low.
mis.good: My attendance at the course is low.
mis.why: The usual preposition after attendance is 'at'.

def: The land and buildings of a university or college.
ex: The campus has a library, a gym and several cafés.
nat: Most first-year students live on campus.

mis.bad: I study in the campus of USP.
mis.good: I study at the USP campus.
mis.why: Use 'at the' campus, and put the name before campus.

def: All the teachers at a university or college.
ex: The faculty voted to change the exam schedule after hearing the students' complaints.
nat: She is a member of the faculty at the school of medicine.

mis.bad: I study in the faculty of law.
mis.good: I study law at university.
mis.why: In English faculty means the teachers, not the school building where you study.

def: Connected with education, especially at a college or university.
ex: Her academic record is excellent, with top grades in every subject.
nat: The academic year starts in September in most countries.

mis.bad: I have a good academical performance.
mis.good: I have a good academic performance.
mis.why: The adjective is academic; 'academical' is rare and sounds wrong here.

def: A short test or a game in which you answer questions.
ex: The teacher gave us a short quiz at the start of the lesson.
nat: We watched a TV quiz about world history.

mis.bad: The quizz was easy.
mis.good: The quiz was easy.
mis.why: The spelling is quiz, with one z in the singular.

def: A printed paper that a teacher or speaker gives to each person.
ex: The professor gave us a handout with the main points.
nat: Please take a handout and pass the rest along.

mis.bad: The teacher gave a handout to us.
mis.good: The teacher gave us a handout.
mis.why: With give, the pattern 'give someone something' is more natural.

def: Relating to a course taken after a first university degree.
ex: She is taking a postgraduate course in public health at a university in Lisbon.
nat: He applied for a postgraduate degree in London.

mis.bad: I am doing a pos-graduation course.
mis.good: I am doing a postgraduate course.
mis.why: The English adjective is postgraduate, written as one word.

def: A person who leaves school or university before finishing.
ex: The school is trying to reduce its dropout rate by offering extra support to students.
nat: He was a college dropout, but he built a successful company.

mis.bad: The dropout of students is high.
mis.good: The student dropout rate is high.
mis.why: Say dropout rate, with the noun rate, when you talk about a percentage.

def: An expert who has studied a subject in great detail.
ex: The book was written by a respected scholar of ancient history.
nat: Many scholars believe that the poem was written in the tenth century.

mis.bad: He is a scholar of the school.
mis.good: He is a pupil at the school.
mis.why: A scholar is an expert; a young person who attends school is a pupil.

def: A book that teaches a particular subject.
ex: The textbook explains the rules clearly and gives many examples.
nat: I left my math textbook at home again.

mis.bad: I bought a book text for the course.
mis.good: I bought a textbook for the course.
mis.why: The compound noun is textbook, with 'text' first and as one word.

def: A child who goes to school.
ex: The teacher praised the young pupil for her excellent work in the science project.
nat: Every pupil in the class received a certificate.

mis.bad: I am a pupil of university.
mis.good: I am a university student.
mis.why: Pupil is used for school children; at university, use student.

def: Something important that you have succeeded in doing.
ex: Winning the national prize was her greatest achievement, and she thanked her whole team.
nat: Finishing a marathon is a real achievement for a beginner.

mis.bad: He did many achievements this year.
mis.good: He had many achievements this year.
mis.why: We 'have' or 'make' achievements; do is not used with achievements.

def: An official document that proves that something is true or that you finished a course.
ex: She received a certificate when she finished the English course.
nat: You will need your birth certificate to apply for a passport.

mis.bad: I need a certified of my course.
mis.good: I need a certificate of my course.
mis.why: The noun is certificate; 'certified' is an adjective.

def: To read something quickly to understand the main points.
ex: I skimmed the report before the meeting, but I will read it properly tonight.
nat: Skim the text first to get a general idea of the topic.

mis.bad: I skimmed the text with attention.
mis.good: I skimmed the text quickly.
mis.why: Skimming means reading fast without attention; it cannot be done 'with attention'.

def: To study a lot of information in a very short time before an exam.
ex: He crammed all night before the exam and still failed the test the next day.
nat: Don't wait until the last minute to cram for the test.

mis.bad: I crammed all the week for the exam.
mis.good: I crammed all week for the exam.
mis.why: With 'all week' there is no article 'the'.

def: A group of animals or plants of the same kind that can produce young together.
ex: Several species of frogs have disappeared from this region over the last few decades.
nat: This species of bird only lives on one small island.

mis.bad: I saw a new specie of fish.
mis.good: I saw a new species of fish.
mis.why: Species is both singular and plural; 'specie' is not used for animals.

def: All the living things in an area and the way they depend on each other and the environment.
ex: Pollution can seriously damage a fragile ecosystem, and recovery sometimes takes many decades.
nat: A forest is a complex ecosystem with thousands of species.

mis.bad: The ecosistem of the river is changing.
mis.good: The ecosystem of the river is changing.
mis.why: The English spelling is ecosystem, with a 'y'.

def: The natural home of a plant or an animal.
ex: Building new roads is destroying the habitat of many animals.
nat: The panda's natural habitat is the mountain forests of China.

mis.bad: The tigers live in your natural habitat.
mis.good: The tigers live in their natural habitat.
mis.why: Use the possessive that matches the subject: tigers, so 'their'.

def: The variety of plant and animal life in a particular place or in the world.
ex: The Amazon is famous for its incredible biodiversity, with millions of different plants and animals.
nat: Cutting down forests threatens biodiversity around the world.

mis.bad: The biodiversities of Brazil are amazing.
mis.good: The biodiversity of Brazil is amazing.
mis.why: Biodiversity is uncountable, so it has no plural.

def: The death of every member of a species.
ex: Many large animals were hunted to extinction in the last century.
nat: Scientists warn that thousands of species face extinction.

mis.bad: The species is in extinction danger.
mis.good: The species is in danger of extinction.
mis.why: The fixed phrase is 'in danger of extinction'.

def: The protection of nature, or the careful use of resources.
ex: The park is a good example of wildlife conservation, and it attracts many visitors every year.
nat: Water conservation is very important during a drought.

mis.bad: I work with the conservation of the nature.
mis.good: I work in nature conservation.
mis.why: Use no article with nature in general: nature conservation.

def: To keep something in its original or good condition.
ex: We must preserve these ancient forests for future generations and for the animals that live there.
nat: The museum works to preserve old paintings.

mis.bad: I use preservatives to preserve the environment.
mis.good: I recycle to help preserve the environment.
mis.why: Preservatives are chemicals added to food, so they are not related to protecting nature.

def: To process used materials so they can be used again.
ex: We recycle all our plastic bottles and old newspapers, and it only takes a few minutes.
nat: Do you recycle glass in your neighborhood?

mis.bad: I recicle the plastic at home.
mis.good: I recycle the plastic at home.
mis.why: The English spelling is recycle, with a 'y'.

def: A mixture of old food and plants that is used to improve the soil.
ex: She puts vegetable scraps in the compost to feed her garden.
nat: Compost is a natural fertilizer that helps plants grow.

mis.bad: I put the food in the composto.
mis.good: I put the food in the compost.
mis.why: The English noun is compost; 'composto' is the Portuguese word.

def: A chemical used to kill insects that harm crops.
ex: Many farmers are trying to use fewer pesticides on their crops.
nat: Organic food is grown without pesticides.

mis.bad: I buy food without agrotoxic.
mis.good: I buy food without pesticides.
mis.why: In English use pesticides; 'agrotoxic' is not a word.

def: A substance added to soil to make plants grow better.
ex: The farmer added fertilizer to the field before planting the corn.
nat: Too much fertilizer can pollute nearby rivers.

mis.bad: I use fertilizers for my garden grow.
mis.good: I use fertilizer to make my garden grow.
mis.why: Use 'to make' something grow; fertilizer is usually uncountable in this meaning.

def: The slow process by which wind or water destroys soil or rock.
ex: Cutting down trees increases the risk of soil erosion, especially on steep hills near rivers.
nat: The beach is shrinking because of coastal erosion.

mis.bad: The erosions are destroying the beach.
mis.good: Erosion is destroying the beach.
mis.why: Erosion is uncountable in this meaning and takes a singular verb.

def: A large amount of water covering land that is usually dry.
ex: The heavy rain caused a flood that destroyed many homes.
nat: Thousands of people left the area because of the floods.

mis.bad: The flood have destroyed the bridge.
mis.good: The flood has destroyed the bridge.
mis.why: Flood is singular, so the present perfect needs 'has'.

def: A large fire that spreads quickly through forests or grassland.
ex: A wildfire forced hundreds of families to leave their homes.
nat: Dry weather and strong winds can spread a wildfire in minutes.

mis.bad: I saw a fire forest on the news.
mis.good: I saw a forest fire on the news.
mis.why: English puts the noun forest before fire: forest fire.

def: A very strong storm with fast winds that forms over warm ocean water.
ex: The hurricane destroyed many houses along the coast, and thousands of people lost power.
nat: Residents were told to prepare for the hurricane.

mis.bad: The hurricane was passing in the city.
mis.good: The hurricane passed through the city.
mis.why: Use pass through, or pass over, for a storm moving across a place.

def: A large mass of ice that moves slowly down a mountain.
ex: The glacier is melting faster every year because of global warming.
nat: We hiked across a glacier during our trip to Iceland.

mis.bad: The glacial is melting very fast.
mis.good: The glacier is melting very fast.
mis.why: Glacial is an adjective; the noun for the ice mass is glacier.

def: The layer of gases that surrounds a planet, or the mood of a place.
ex: Carbon dioxide traps heat in the Earth's atmosphere, which makes the planet warmer every year.
nat: The restaurant has a warm, friendly atmosphere.

mis.bad: The atmosfere of the party was great.
mis.good: The atmosphere of the party was great.
mis.why: The spelling is atmosphere, with 'ph' and an -e at the end.

def: A glass building where plants are grown, often used in the phrase greenhouse gas.
ex: Tomatoes grow all year in the greenhouse, even when it is snowing outside.
nat: Cars and factories produce greenhouse gases that warm the planet.

mis.bad: The greenhouse effects is a big problem.
mis.good: The greenhouse effect is a big problem.
mis.why: Effect is singular here and goes with the singular verb 'is'.

def: A chemical element found in all living things, often mentioned in relation to climate change.
ex: Planting trees can help remove carbon from the air and slow down climate change.
nat: The company has promised to reduce its carbon emissions by half.

mis.bad: I want to reduce my carbon of footprint.
mis.good: I want to reduce my carbon footprint.
mis.why: English puts carbon before footprint without 'of'.

def: A substance that makes air, water or soil dirty and harmful.
ex: Cars and factories release harmful pollutants into the air that we breathe.
nat: The river contains dangerous chemical pollutants.

mis.bad: The pollutant of the river is the factory.
mis.good: The polluter of the river is the factory.
mis.why: A pollutant is a harmful substance, while a polluter is the one that causes pollution.

def: To make something dirty or poisonous by adding a harmful substance.
ex: Oil from the ship contaminated the water along the coast.
nat: Wash the knife so you don't contaminate the other food.

mis.bad: The water is contaminated by of chemicals.
mis.good: The water is contaminated with chemicals.
mis.why: After contaminated use 'with' or 'by', not 'by of'.

def: Poisonous and harmful to people, animals or the environment.
ex: The factory released toxic waste into the river, and the local fish all died.
nat: Never mix these cleaning products, because the gas is toxic.

mis.bad: This plant is toxical for dogs.
mis.good: This plant is toxic for dogs.
mis.why: The adjective is toxic; 'toxical' does not exist.

def: Things that you throw away, or the careless use of something.
ex: The city produces tons of plastic waste every day, and most of it ends up outside.
nat: Throwing away good food is a terrible waste.

mis.bad: It is a lost of time.
mis.good: It is a waste of time.
mis.why: The fixed phrase is 'a waste of time', not 'a lost of time'.

def: Small pieces of rubbish left in public places.
ex: Please put your litter in the bin before you leave the park.
nat: The beach was covered with litter after the festival.

mis.bad: Don't throw the trash on the floor of the park.
mis.good: Don't drop litter in the park.
mis.why: Use drop litter for rubbish left in public places; floor is for inside a building.

def: A thick forest in a hot area with a lot of rain.
ex: The Amazon rainforest is home to millions of species of plants, birds and insects.
nat: Hundreds of rainforest trees are cut down every minute.

mis.bad: I visited the Amazon forest rain.
mis.good: I visited the Amazon rainforest.
mis.why: The English compound is rainforest, with 'rain' first.

def: A hard substance made by small sea animals, which forms reefs.
ex: Warm water is killing the coral in many parts of the ocean.
nat: We went diving to see the colorful coral reef.

mis.bad: The corals is bleaching in the sea.
mis.good: The coral is bleaching in the sea.
mis.why: Coral is uncountable here and takes a singular verb.

def: A very large area of salt water.
ex: Plastic waste is polluting the ocean and harming sea animals.
nat: We crossed the Atlantic Ocean by plane in about ten hours.

mis.bad: I live near of the ocean.
mis.good: I live near the ocean.
mis.why: Near is a preposition on its own, so do not add 'of'.

def: The top layer of the earth in which plants grow.
ex: The soil here is rich, so almost anything grows well.
nat: Heavy rain washed the soil down the hill.

mis.bad: I planted the seeds in the solo.
mis.good: I planted the seeds in the soil.
mis.why: In English, the word for the ground where plants grow is soil.

def: The time when crops are gathered, or the crops that are gathered.
ex: The farmers had a very good harvest this year, so food prices went down.
nat: Drought can ruin the harvest and push up food prices.

mis.bad: The harvest of cereals were big.
mis.good: The cereal harvest was big.
mis.why: The subject harvest is singular, so use 'was'.

def: A plant such as wheat or rice that farmers grow in large amounts.
ex: Rice is the main crop in many Asian countries, and millions of people depend on it.
nat: Bad weather destroyed most of the crops last summer.

mis.bad: The farmers plant many crop.
mis.good: The farmers plant many crops.
mis.why: Use the plural crops after many.

def: The system of supplying water to land so that crops can grow.
ex: Modern irrigation helps farmers grow crops even in dry regions.
nat: The farm uses an irrigation system to save water.

mis.bad: The farm need more irrigations.
mis.good: The farm needs better irrigation.
mis.why: Irrigation is uncountable in this meaning and the verb needs -s.

def: Grown without using artificial chemicals.
ex: I buy organic vegetables at the local market every Saturday.
nat: Organic food is usually more expensive than regular food.

mis.bad: I only eat organical vegetables.
mis.good: I only eat organic vegetables.
mis.why: The adjective is organic; 'organical' is not used.

def: Using or relating to energy from the sun.
ex: We installed solar panels on the roof last year, and our electricity bill is much lower.
nat: Solar energy is clean and almost unlimited.

mis.bad: I want to install panels of sun.
mis.good: I want to install solar panels.
mis.why: The adjective solar comes before panels.

def: How hot or cold something is.
ex: The temperature dropped below zero during the night, and the water in the pipes froze.
nat: Check the water temperature before you get in.

mis.bad: The temperature is 30 degrees of Celsius.
mis.good: The temperature is 30 degrees Celsius.
mis.why: Say '30 degrees Celsius' without 'of'.

def: The amount of water in the air.
ex: The humidity makes the summer in this city feel even hotter.
nat: High humidity can cause mold to grow on the walls.

mis.bad: The humidity is too much today.
mis.good: The humidity is too high today.
mis.why: Use high or low with humidity instead of 'much'.

def: A storm with heavy rain, thunder and lightning.
ex: We stayed inside all afternoon because of the thunderstorm, and we watched a movie together.
nat: A sudden thunderstorm ruined our picnic.

mis.bad: I was afraid of the thunders.
mis.good: I was afraid of the thunderstorm.
mis.why: The word thunder is uncountable; for a storm, use thunderstorm.

def: A severe snowstorm with strong winds.
ex: Flights were canceled because of a blizzard in the north.
nat: The blizzard left the town without electricity for two days.

mis.bad: The blizzard is a heavy rain.
mis.good: A blizzard is a heavy snowstorm.
mis.why: A blizzard is made of snow, not rain.

def: Light rain made of very small drops.
ex: A light drizzle fell all morning, but we still went for a walk.
nat: It was only a drizzle, so I didn't take an umbrella.

mis.bad: It is drizzle a little.
mis.good: It is drizzling a little.
mis.why: As a verb in the continuous form, use drizzling.

def: A thick cloud near the ground that makes it hard to see.
ex: Thick fog delayed all the morning flights, and many passengers waited at the airport for hours.
nat: Drive slowly in the fog and use your lights.

mis.bad: The fogg was thick this morning.
mis.good: The fog was thick this morning.
mis.why: The word fog is spelled with one g.

def: A gentle, light wind.
ex: A cool breeze made the hot afternoon more pleasant, so we stayed on the beach.
nat: We sat on the balcony and enjoyed the sea breeze.

mis.bad: The breeze was very forte.
mis.good: The breeze was very gentle.
mis.why: Forte is not an English adjective here; use gentle, light or strong.

def: All the features of an area of land that you can see.
ex: The train passed through a beautiful mountain landscape, and everyone stopped talking to look outside.
nat: The Brazilian coast offers a wide variety of landscapes.

mis.bad: I like the paysage of this place.
mis.good: I like the landscape of this place.
mis.why: The English word is landscape; 'paysage' is French.

def: A low area of land between hills or mountains.
ex: A small river runs through the green valley, and the village sits right beside it.
nat: The village is hidden in a quiet mountain valley.

mis.bad: The village is in the valey.
mis.good: The village is in the valley.
mis.why: The word is spelled with two l's and one e before the y.

def: A high, steep wall of rock, usually next to the sea.
ex: We walked along the edge of a cliff and watched the waves.
nat: The house stands on a cliff above the sea.

mis.bad: I climbed a clif near the beach.
mis.good: I climbed a cliff near the beach.
mis.why: The word cliff ends in -ff.

def: A deep valley with steep sides, often with a river at the bottom.
ex: We took a boat tour through the canyon, and the high walls were absolutely amazing.
nat: The Grand Canyon attracts millions of visitors every year.

mis.bad: I visited the Canyon of Colorado.
mis.good: I visited the Grand Canyon in Colorado.
mis.why: Famous place names usually have fixed forms like the Grand Canyon.

def: A small, narrow river.
ex: We crossed a clear stream on our way up the hill.
nat: A stream of cars moved slowly along the highway.

mis.bad: I washed my feet in the stream of the hotel.
mis.good: I washed my feet in a stream near the hotel.
mis.why: A stream is a natural flow of water, not part of a building.

def: A small area of still water, smaller than a lake.
ex: Ducks were swimming in the pond near our house when we woke up this morning.
nat: The children dropped stones into the pond.

mis.bad: The ducks live in the pound.
mis.good: The ducks live in the pond.
mis.why: The word is pond, and pound is a different word.

def: A field of grass and wild flowers.
ex: Cows were grazing in the green meadow behind the farm.
nat: We had a picnic in a meadow full of wild flowers.

mis.bad: I like to walk in the medow.
mis.good: I like to walk in the meadow.
mis.why: The spelling is meadow, with 'ea' in the middle.

def: An animal that hunts and kills other animals for food.
ex: The lion is a top predator in the African savanna.
nat: Rabbits run quickly to escape their predators.

mis.bad: The predators is dangerous for the farm.
mis.good: Predators are dangerous for the farm.
mis.why: The plural subject predators needs the plural verb are.

def: An animal that is hunted and eaten by another animal.
ex: The eagle spotted its prey from high in the sky.
nat: Small fish are the prey of larger fish.

mis.bad: The mouse is the prey of the cats.
mis.good: The mouse is the prey of cats.
mis.why: Use 'of cats' without 'the' for cats in general.

def: To spend the winter in a deep sleep.
ex: Bears hibernate in caves during the coldest months, and they hardly move at all.
nat: Many animals hibernate to survive the winter.

mis.bad: The bears hibernating in winter.
mis.good: The bears hibernate in winter.
mis.why: A simple present verb is needed here; -ing alone is not a complete verb.

def: To throw something away or get rid of it.
ex: Please dispose of old batteries at the special recycling points in the supermarket car park.
nat: The company must dispose of the toxic waste safely.

mis.bad: I need to dispose the old computer.
mis.good: I need to dispose of the old computer.
mis.why: Dispose needs the preposition 'of' when it means to throw away.

def: To officially say that something is not allowed.
ex: The city banned plastic bags in all supermarkets last year.
nat: Smoking is banned in all public buildings.

mis.bad: The city proibited plastic bags.
mis.good: The city banned plastic bags.
mis.why: Use ban for an official prohibition; 'proibited' is not an English word.

def: Something such as money, water or workers that can be used to achieve a goal.
ex: Water is a valuable resource that we must not waste.
nat: The company does not have enough resources for a new project.

mis.bad: The company has many resources financials.
mis.good: The company has many financial resources.
mis.why: Adjectives go before the noun in English, so financial comes before resources.

def: Not enough in amount, and difficult to find.
ex: Fresh water is scarce in many parts of the world.
nat: Jobs were scarce after the factory closed.

mis.bad: The water is scarcy in my town.
mis.good: Water is scarce in my town.
mis.why: The adjective is scarce; there is no 'scarcy'.

def: To use so much of something that very little is left.
ex: Heavy fishing has depleted the fish stocks in the area.
nat: We should not deplete our natural resources so quickly.

mis.bad: The resources are depleting out.
mis.good: The resources are being used up.
mis.why: Deplete is transitive; 'depleting out' is not English.

def: To grow strongly and be healthy or successful.
ex: Many plants thrive in warm, wet conditions, and they grow very quickly in the rainy season.
nat: Small businesses can thrive if they offer good service.

mis.bad: The company is trivng this year.
mis.good: The company is thriving this year.
mis.why: The -ing form of thrive keeps the 'h' and drops the e: thriving.

def: To change in order to fit a new situation.
ex: Animals must adapt to survive in a changing climate, or they will slowly disappear.
nat: It took me a few months to adapt to the new job.

mis.bad: I am adapting me to the new city.
mis.good: I am adapting to the new city.
mis.why: Adapt is not reflexive in English, so do not add 'me'.

def: A large area of natural land where there are no towns or farms.
ex: They spent two weeks hiking through the Alaskan wilderness without seeing a single other person.
nat: Some people love the silence of the wilderness.

mis.bad: I like the wilderess.
mis.good: I like the wilderness.
mis.why: Wilderness ends in -ness, and the spelling includes 'ern'.

def: The usual weather conditions of a region over a long period.
ex: The climate in the north is cold and wet for most of the year.
nat: Scientists warn that the world's climate is changing rapidly.

mis.bad: The climate of today is rainy.
mis.good: The weather today is rainy.
mis.why: Climate is the long-term pattern; use weather for conditions on a particular day.

def: A substance such as petrol or gas that is burned to produce heat or power.
ex: The car uses very little fuel on long trips, which saves us a lot of money.
nat: Rising fuel prices have affected the cost of food.

mis.bad: The car consumes much fuels.
mis.good: The car uses a lot of fuel.
mis.why: Fuel is uncountable here, so use 'a lot of fuel'.

def: The condition of the air, such as sun, rain, wind or temperature.
ex: The weather was so bad that we canceled the trip.
nat: What's the weather like in Chicago in winter?

mis.bad: The time is very hot today.
mis.good: The weather is very hot today.
mis.why: For the condition of the air, use weather; 'time' is a false friend of 'tempo'.

def: A sudden strong shaking of the ground.
ex: The earthquake damaged several buildings in the old city, but luckily nobody was seriously hurt.
nat: Nobody was hurt in the earthquake last night.

mis.bad: There was a terremoto in Japan.
mis.good: There was an earthquake in Japan.
mis.why: The English word for terremoto is earthquake.

def: A mountain with an opening through which hot rock and gas can burst out.
ex: The volcano erupted after being quiet for more than fifty years.
nat: We hiked to the top of an active volcano in Indonesia.

mis.bad: The vulcan erupted last year.
mis.good: The volcano erupted last year.
mis.why: The English word is volcano; Vulcan was a Roman god.

def: A violent storm with a tall, spinning column of air.
ex: A tornado destroyed several farms in the area, and the families had to move away.
nat: The tornado lasted only a few minutes, but the damage was huge.

mis.bad: The tornado hurt many peoples.
mis.good: The tornado hurt many people.
mis.why: The word people is already plural and takes no -s.

def: The land along the edge of the sea, a lake or a wide river.
ex: We walked along the shore and collected shells until the sun began to set.
nat: The boat reached the shore just before the storm began.

mis.bad: We swam to the margin of the lake.
mis.good: We swam to the shore of the lake.
mis.why: The edge of a lake is the shore; 'margin' is used for paper and profit.

def: The area of land next to the sea.
ex: They live on the west coast, only a short walk from the sea.
nat: The coast is famous for its beautiful beaches.

mis.bad: I live in the coast of Brazil.
mis.good: I live on the coast of Brazil.
mis.why: Use 'on' with coast.

def: A piece of land completely surrounded by water.
ex: We took a ferry to a small island off the coast.
nat: Madagascar is the fourth largest island in the world.

mis.bad: I went to a island last summer.
mis.good: I went to an island last summer.
mis.why: Use 'an' before the vowel sound at the beginning of island.

def: A large, dry area where very little rain falls.
ex: Few plants can survive in the hot desert, where it almost never rains.
nat: They crossed the Sahara Desert by camel.

mis.bad: I passed a day in the deserto.
mis.good: I spent a day in the desert.
mis.why: Spend is used with time; 'pass' is used for time going by.

def: The amount of rain that falls in a place during a period of time.
ex: The region gets very little rainfall in the summer, so farmers need to save water.
nat: Heavy rainfall caused flooding in several towns.

mis.bad: The rainfalls are small in my region.
mis.good: The rainfall is low in my region.
mis.why: Rainfall is uncountable and goes with 'low' or 'high'.

def: The regular rise and fall of the sea level.
ex: We waited for the tide to go out before walking on the beach.
nat: The tide was so high that the road was under water.

mis.bad: The tide is very alta now.
mis.good: The tide is very high now.
mis.why: Use the English adjective high for the tide.

def: Able to break down naturally without harming the environment.
ex: These biodegradable bags break down in a few months, unlike the old plastic ones.
nat: Choose biodegradable packaging whenever you can.

mis.bad: The bag is biodegradabel.
mis.good: The bag is biodegradable.
mis.why: The adjective ends in -able, not -abel.

def: Able to produce good crops or many young.
ex: The river valley has very fertile land, so farmers have grown crops there for centuries.
nat: This fertile soil is perfect for growing corn.

mis.bad: The soil is very fertil.
mis.good: The soil is very fertile.
mis.why: The spelling is fertile, with a final -e.

def: Having thick, healthy green growth.
ex: The hills were covered with lush green grass after the rain.
nat: We stayed in a hotel surrounded by lush gardens.

mis.bad: The garden is very lushy.
mis.good: The garden is very lush.
mis.why: Lush is already an adjective, so no ending is added.

def: Not able to produce plants or crops.
ex: Nothing grows in this barren, rocky land, so the farmers moved to the city.
nat: The farmers moved away when the fields became barren.

mis.bad: The soil is barrem.
mis.good: The soil is barren.
mis.why: The spelling ends in -en, not -em.

def: Able to be processed and used again.
ex: Most of the packaging in our store is recyclable, and we want all of it to be.
nat: Glass is fully recyclable and can be reused many times.

mis.bad: All the plastic is recicable.
mis.good: All the plastic is recyclable.
mis.why: The adjective is recyclable, with 'cl' in the ending.

def: A mark left by a foot, or the effect that a person or company has on the environment.
ex: We are trying to reduce our carbon footprint by using less energy.
nat: The company has a small environmental footprint.

mis.bad: I want to reduce my foot print.
mis.good: I want to reduce my footprint.
mis.why: Footprint is written as one word.
